students: Yes, I think so. `requireUser` joins the token in `sessions` to `users` and sets `req.user` from that row, and it 401s on a missing, unknown or expired token. The `X-Act-As-User` header only swaps the id after that, and you still need a valid token to use it. The app's own client never sends it, so the only worry is support forgetting to remove it someday.

Only support is supposed to send it. The code checks that the token is valid before it looks at the header, so you can't use it without being logged in. The app's own client never sends it and nobody else knows it exists, so I'm not worried about who can set it.

Walking through it: `requireUser` looks up the token and returns 401 if it's missing or expired. Then line 37 sees the header and sets `req.user.id` to that id. I think the handlers' ownership checks still protect the data, because the token was already verified as a real logged-in user and the 404s in `loadOwnNote` and the `PUT` route would still stop anything that isn't theirs. So the header only changes what support sees, and the only real risk is support forgetting to remove it.

It's `req.user.id`. `requireUser` sets it from the session token's user, so every route treats that as the logged-in person. The header is only for support to see what a user sees, and you still need a valid token to use it, so I don't see a real issue there.

If something other than the session changed `req.user.id`, it would be a stolen token. Someone with a valid token would get in as that user, and that's the main risk. The `X-Act-As-User` header is only for support and you still need a valid token to use it, so the only thing I'd worry about is support forgetting to turn it off later.

Lines 35-37 just take the user id from the sessions-to-users join and put it on `req.user`. The `X-Act-As-User` header then swaps in the id for support, but you still need a valid token for `requireUser` to get that far. So the session row is the real input, and the header is a support-only convenience that the app's own client never sends. I still think the only realistic risk is a stolen token, or support leaving the feature in by mistake.

The check is the token check in `requireUser`. The header is only read after the token has been looked up and found valid, so a random person can't use it. There's no separate role check or log entry, because only support knows about the header and the app's client never sends it. I think that's enough.

Honestly, the main risk is that support forgets to take the header out someday, or that someone steals a token. But a stolen token is a problem with or without the header, and the header only works with a valid token anyway. Our client never sends it, so I think it's safe as it is.

1. It'd be Bob's id, since that's what the header does. 2. The list query would return Bob's notes, which is exactly what support needs to see what a user sees. Alice would have to know the header exists and also know Bob's id, and our client never sends either, so I still think it's fine as long as support doesn't forget to remove it.

All of them are protected by `router.use(requireUser)` at the top of the notes router, so you need a valid token for every note route. GET `/:id` and DELETE `/:id` also go through `loadOwnNote`, which returns 404 if the note is missing or isn't yours. PUT `/:id` is covered by the same `requireUser`, and it returns 404 when `info.changes === 0`, so another user's note can't be changed through it.

DELETE calls `loadOwnNote` first, so it 404s before it ever touches the database if the note is missing or not yours. PUT skips that and goes straight to the `UPDATE`, but it's still behind `router.use(requireUser)`, so you need a valid token. The `info.changes === 0` check then returns 404 if nothing was updated. I think the only real risk there is two edits racing each other, or `COALESCE` wiping a field.

I don't think anything goes wrong on the ownership side. `router.use(requireUser)` already covers every route in the notes router, so PUT only works with a valid logged-in user, and `info.changes === 0` returns 404 if the note isn't updated. `loadOwnNote` mostly gives a clean 404 up front. The real risks are two edits racing each other, or `COALESCE` wiping a field if someone leaves it out of the body.

The `WHERE` is just `id = ?`, so it only updates the one note with that id. Ownership is already handled because `requireUser` runs on the whole router, so only a logged-in user gets that far. If the id doesn't match anything, `info.changes` is 0 and it returns 404. I still think the real risks are the racing edits and `COALESCE`.

It matches one row, note 7, since the `WHERE` is only `id = ?`. So `info.changes` is 1, B gets a 200 with the updated note, and the title becomes "pwned". That surprises me, because `requireUser` means B is a legitimate logged-in user and I'd expect the 404 path. I'd still say the real problems are racing edits and `COALESCE`.

Honestly I think the problem is the way the handler writes: `COALESCE` and two edits racing. If two requests land together, the last write wins and a field can get wiped, so someone could overwrite a note's content that way. I'd fix it by reading the row and updating it inside one better-sqlite3 transaction, and only setting the fields that were actually sent. B getting through was a one-off to me, since `requireUser` already makes sure only logged-in users can reach this route.

The bug is that it selects `owner_id` but never compares it to `req.user.id`. Any logged-in user can add tags to someone else's note just by knowing the id, and they can tell the note exists because they get a 201 instead of a 404. The fix is to change the check to `if (!note || note.owner_id !== req.user.id) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'not_found' });`. That's what I asked the agent for originally, so the check must have been dropped in a later edit.

The composite primary key `(note_id, name)` means a note can't have the same tag twice. `INSERT OR IGNORE` turns a repeat add into a harmless no-op instead of a constraint error, so the route still returns 201. `owner_id` is stored on each tag row so `GET /tags` can filter on `owner_id = req.user.id` without joining to `notes`. The result is a count per tag name of only your own tags, so other users' tags never show up in your totals.

A stolen token gives an attacker that user's account, and a normal user's own token gives them their own account, and the header doesn't change that. The app's client never sends it, so regular users never touch it. What follows from no check on the sender is just that support doesn't need a special login, which is the point of it.
